kicker: Ember · Science · Test on Wed 18 Nov
title: Day 5: Breathing
sub: Day 5 (Sun). Breathing in and out, the bell-jar model and lung volume. It links straight back to gas pressure (Day 2). About 25 minutes.
skill: The Because Chain: cause → effect → consequence.
target: The breathing chain always runs: muscles move → chest volume changes → pressure changes → air moves. Miss the pressure link and you miss marks.

blocks.html:
Inhaling (breathing in)
  • Muscles between the ribs contract: the ribcage moves up and out.
  • The diaphragm contracts and moves down.
  • The volume inside the chest increases.
  • The pressure inside the chest decreases, so air is drawn in.
Exhaling (breathing out)
  • Rib muscles relax: the ribcage moves down and in.
  • The diaphragm relaxes and moves up.
  • Chest volume decreases; pressure increases, so air is pushed out.
Link to Day 2: a bigger volume means the gas particles hit the walls less often, so the pressure falls. Air always moves from higher pressure to lower pressure.

blocks.q: What does your ribcage do when you inhale?
blocks.why: Rib muscles contract, pulling the ribs up and out.

blocks.q: What does the diaphragm do when you exhale?
blocks.why: Breathing out: the diaphragm relaxes and domes up.

blocks.q: When you inhale, what happens to the pressure inside your chest?
blocks.why: The volume gets bigger, so the pressure drops below the air outside, and air flows in.

blocks.h: Inhaling: put the steps in order
blocks.q: Tap the steps of breathing in, in order.
items: The rib muscles and diaphragm contract.
The ribcage moves up and out and the diaphragm moves down.
The volume of the chest increases.
The pressure in the chest decreases.
Air is drawn into the lungs.
blocks.done: Muscles → volume up → pressure down → air in.

sections.h: 2. The bell-jar model and lung volume

blocks.html:
The bell-jar model: the jar = the chest, the balloons = the lungs, the rubber sheet = the diaphragm.
Pull the sheet down → volume in the jar increases → pressure decreases → air rushes in → the balloons inflate (like inhaling). Push it up → the balloons deflate.
A problem with the model: the jar’s sides cannot move, but the real ribcage moves up and out.

Lung volume is measured by breathing out fully through a tube into an upside-down bottle full of water: the volume of water pushed out = the air your lungs held. Regular exercise can increase lung volume. Smoking, asthma and old age can reduce it.

blocks.q: In the bell-jar model, what does the rubber sheet represent?
blocks.why: Balloons = lungs, jar = chest, rubber sheet = diaphragm.

blocks.q: You pull the rubber sheet down. What happens to the balloons, and why?
o: They deflate, because the pressure in the jar rises
They inflate, because the volume in the jar increases and the pressure decreases, so air rushes in
blocks.why: Same chain as inhaling: volume up → pressure down → air in.

blocks.q: Which is a problem with the bell-jar model?
o: The jar cannot move, but the real ribcage moves up and out
blocks.why: The model only shows the diaphragm’s part, not the ribs.
Smoking, asthma and old age can reduce lung volume.

blocks.q: Explain how changes in volume and pressure inside the chest move air into and out of the lungs.

points.t: breathing in: rib muscles contract, ribs move up and out
so the chest volume increases and the pressure decreases
so air is drawn in (from higher pressure outside)
breathing out: muscles relax, ribs move down and in, diaphragm moves up
so the volume decreases, the pressure increases and air is pushed out

mark.note: A 6-mark explain: give the whole chain for both breathing in and breathing out. The pressure link earns marks.

starters: When you breathe in, the muscles between your ribs…
This increases the volume, so the pressure…

blocks.q: Describe how you would measure the lung volume of an athlete.

points.t: fill a bottle (or tank) with water and turn it upside down in water
the athlete takes a deep breath and breathes out fully through a tube into the bottle
the volume of water pushed out = the lung volume

starters: First, fill a bottle with water…

items: I can give the full chain for breathing in: muscles → volume up → pressure down → air in.
I can give the reverse for breathing out.
I know what each part of the bell-jar model stands for, and one problem with it.
I can describe how to measure lung volume.
I can name three things that reduce lung volume.

blocks.q: “What happens to the pressure in your chest when you breathe in, and why does that make air go in?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for volume increases → pressure decreases → air moves in from higher pressure outside. If she says “the lungs suck air in”, ask “what happens to the pressure?”
